summary.text: Statistics is the discipline of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting and presenting data.
When data on every member of a population cannot be collected, statisticians use survey samples and experiment designs, and random sampling lets conclusions reasonably extend to the whole population.
Descriptive statistics summarize a sample, while inferential statistics draw conclusions from data subject to random variation.

items.prompt: A city cannot ask all of its residents about a new park. What lets answers from some residents reasonably extend to everyone?

options.label: Waiting until a census is possible

items.explain: When a census cannot be collected, random sampling assures that conclusions can reasonably extend from the sample to the whole population.

items.prompt: Researchers measure a group of plants, change how much water they get, then measure them again the same way. What kind of study is this?
items.explain: An experimental study involves manipulating the system and measuring again; an observational study involves no manipulation.

items.prompt: A pollster questions 1,000 voters to make statements about a whole country. Which method of data analysis is that?
items.explain: Inferential statistics draws conclusions about a population from a sample, unlike descriptive statistics, which summarize the sample.

items.prompt: A test says a medicine works, though in truth it does nothing. Which kind of error is that?
items.explain: A Type I error is when the null hypothesis is rejected though it is in fact true, a false positive.

items.prompt: A survey records each person's favourite colour. What kind of data is that?
items.explain: Data may be a numerical value (quantitative) or a label (qualitative).

items.prompt: An analyst reports weights in pounds while everyone believes they are in kilograms. What kind of error is that?
items.explain: Errors can be random (noise), systematic (bias), or other types such as a blunder, for example reporting incorrect units.

steps.text: We want to learn about everyone in a country.
We cannot collect data from every member.
So we survey a sample chosen at random.
Therefore the results describe only those surveyed and can never reasonably extend to the country.

paragraphs.heading: What statistics is
paragraphs.text: Statistics is the discipline of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting and presenting data. Data can be numerical values, called quantitative data, or labels, called qualitative data. The name comes from the German Statistik, which first meant a description of a state or a country.

paragraphs.heading: Populations and samples
paragraphs.text: A statistical study usually begins with a statistical population or a statistical model. A population can be any group of people or objects, from everyone living in a country to every atom in a crystal. When a census covering every member is not possible, statisticians design experiments and survey samples instead. Random sampling is what lets conclusions drawn from a sample reasonably extend to the whole population.

paragraphs.heading: Experiments and observation
paragraphs.text: Two kinds of study are set against each other here. In an experimental study you measure a system, change something about it, then measure again in the same way to see whether the change altered the results. An observational study leaves out that manipulation.

paragraphs.heading: Describing and inferring
paragraphs.text: Analysis uses two main kinds of method. Descriptive statistics summarize a sample with measures such as the mean or the standard deviation. They mostly look at central tendency, the typical or central value, and dispersion, how far members spread from the center and from each other. Inferential statistics use a sample to make statements and predictions about the population, in the face of random variation such as observational errors and sampling variation.

paragraphs.heading: Testing hypotheses
paragraphs.text: A standard procedure tests whether two data sets are related. The idealized default, called the null hypothesis, says there is no relationship, and statistical tests measure the sense in which the data show it to be false. Two basic mistakes are possible. A Type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false positive; a Type II error fails to reject one that is actually false, a false negative.

paragraphs.heading: The science of uncertainty
paragraphs.text: Statistics rests on probability, the branch of mathematics that studies random events, yet the two are distinct. Probability deduces answers for particular situations from a general theory, while statistics works the other way, inducing statements about a population from a data set. Statistics is often called the science of uncertainty, a name that reflects how it copes with measurement and sampling errors and with uncertainty in modelling.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: The word traces back to the Latin status, meaning situation or condition, which in late Latin came to mean state. From it the political scientist Gottfried Achenwall coined the German statistik. The term reached English in 1770, meaning the study of political arrangements, and took on its modern sense in the 1790s in the works of John Sinclair.
